finding.claim: GET /users returns the id and name of every user in whatever org the caller names. The org comes from the query string and nothing checks that the caller is authenticated or belongs to that org. This is a candidate broken-access-control / IDOR issue. Confidence is moderate, because authentication may be applied by middleware outside this file that sets req.pg. No such middleware is visible in this directory.
finding.sink: req.pg.query("SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE org = $1") with the result returned via res.json(rows)

trace.note: Route handler registered with no auth or authorization middleware (app.use is never called)
req.query.org is passed directly as the tenant filter. The caller's identity or org is never compared with it.
Matching rows are returned to the caller

finding.guards_checked: The SQL is parameterized ($1), so there is no SQL injection. No authentication or session middleware, no org-membership check and no rate limiting appear anywhere in db.js. Other routes were also reviewed: /file normalizes with path.resolve and enforces a ROOT+sep prefix check, so traversal is blocked (symlinks inside public/ would be a caveat). /count uses execFile with fixed arguments, so there is no command injection.

verdict.reason: db.js:8-10 matches the trace, and the only file in the directory has no auth, session or org-membership check (the SQL at db.js:9 is parameterized). However, `req.pg` is never set anywhere (no `app.use`), so the handler would throw as written, and whether a deployment adds auth or a pg-attaching middleware can't be determined from this code.

verdict_facts.guard_found: none (the query is parameterized, which stops SQL injection but not the missing org-membership check; the handler never reads req.user)
verdict_facts.reason: db.js:8-10 registers /users with no auth or authorization check, and db.js:9 filters on the attacker-supplied req.query.org without comparing it to any caller identity, so any HTTP client can list any org's users.
